network.overall_strategy: Use the experimentally supported cyanosulfidic surface network of Patel et al. (2015) rather than inventing unsupported hydrothermal or biochemical detours. Acetylene and HCN generate acrylonitrile, ammonia and cyanamide build the aminonitrile and guanidine motifs, Cu/H2S-assisted cyclization forms a hexahydropyrimidine hub, HCN ring opening and sulfide-driven nitrile-thioamide editing install the full carbon skeleton, and final amination plus aqueous nitrile hydrolysis yield racemic arginine. Hydrothermal or volcanic systems are treated only as plausible sources of H2S, HCN, acetylene, and copper because the arginine-forming chemistry itself is best supported in surface cyanosulfidic pools. Because only one full feedstock-to-target family is well supported, the 10 listed pathways comprise three experimentally distinct full routes and seven valid downstream routes from experimentally observed hub intermediates.

reactions.name: Hydrocyanation of acetylene to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic cyanosulfidic evaporitic pool or shoreline film; concentration by evaporation and local UV shielding favor survival of HCN adducts.

reactions.mechanism: HCN adds across the C-C triple bond of acetylene to give the vinyl nitrile acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the documented entry step of the cyanosulfidic arginine sequence and efficiently converts two plausible atmospheric or volcanic feedstocks into a three-carbon activated nitrile (Patel et al., 2015). In surface settings the main challenge is maintaining sufficient local HCN concentration while limiting destructive UV side chemistry.

reactions.name: Michael addition of ammonia to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Mildly basic, NH3-rich cyanosulfidic pool under wet-dry cycling.

reactions.mechanism: Conjugate 1,4-addition of ammonia to the beta-carbon of acrylonitrile yields the beta-amino nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) place this Michael addition directly after acrylonitrile formation in the arginine sequence. The step is chemically favorable because acrylonitrile is an activated Michael acceptor, though hydrolysis and oligomerization remain plausible side reactions in surface pools.

reactions.name: Guanidination of 3-aminopropanenitrile with cyanamide

conditions.other: Wet-dry concentration enhances cyanamide capture by the amino nitrile.

reactions.mechanism: The primary amine attacks cyanamide and forms the guanidine-amidine linkage characteristic of arginine.
reactions.reasoning: This is the decisive arginine-specific functionalization in the Patel et al. (2015) network because it installs the guanidino motif absent from other amino acid routes. The literature review also highlights uncertainty over sustained prebiotic cyanamide concentrations, so this is a plausible supply bottleneck.

reactions.name: Dry Cu/H2S cyclization to 4-hydroxy-2-iminohexahydropyrimidine

conditions.other: Partially dry anoxic mineral film on Cu-bearing grains in an H2S-rich surface setting.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular attack of a guanidine nitrogen on the nitrile closes a six-membered ring; Cu/H2S assists formation of the cyclic hemiaminal.
reactions.reasoning: This is one of the three experimentally reported Cu/H2S-assisted cyclization variants in Patel et al. (2015). The dry variant is geochemically sensible in evaporitic films where concentration and reduced copper can promote intramolecular attack, although early-Earth access to native copper remains debated.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic Cu/H2S cyclization to 4-hydroxy-2-iminohexahydropyrimidine

conditions.other: Shallow anoxic surface pool with Cu-bearing grains and dissolved sulfide.

reactions.mechanism: The same intramolecular ring closure occurs as in the dry variant, but water assists nitrile hydration to the C4 hydroxylated hemiaminal.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) also reported a hydrolytic Cu/H2S cyclization variant. Keeping it separate preserves the experimentally observed ambiguity between dry-film and aqueous ring closure under cyanosulfidic surface conditions.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic Cu/H2S cyclization with ammonia release

conditions.other: Shallow anoxic surface pool with Cu-bearing grains and dissolved sulfide.

reactions.mechanism: Water-assisted ring closure and hydration produce the cyclic hemiaminal with net NH3 release.
reactions.reasoning: This third documented cyclization variant from Patel et al. (2015) differs by net ammonia release and therefore creates an internal nitrogen recycle within the network. Like the other cyclizations, however, it depends on Cu/H2S conditions whose geochemical availability may have been patchy.

reactions.name: HCN ring opening of the hexahydropyrimidine

conditions.other: HCN-rich anoxic pool intermittently concentrated by evaporation.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the hemiaminal carbon, opens the ring, and generates a linear cyanohydrin-guanidine.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) used HCN to reopen the cyclic hemiaminal and thereby homologate the carbon skeleton. This is a crucial step, but the review notes that regioselectivity of the C4 opening is still not fully resolved.

reactions.name: Nitrile thiolysis to the hydroxy-thioamide

conditions.other: Sulfide-rich surface water with limited oxidants and reduced sulfur input from volcanic or geothermal sources.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogen sulfide adds across the nitrile to form the corresponding thioamide while retaining the adjacent hydroxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: The nitrile-to-thioamide conversion is a hallmark cyanosulfidic transformation and was experimentally demonstrated in the arginine route by Patel et al. (2015). Sulfide-rich surface waters make the chemistry plausible, though the reactive cyanohydrin and thioamide intermediates would benefit from partial UV shielding.

reactions.name: Reductive dehydroxylation of the hydroxy-thioamide

conditions.other: Dry-down or mineral-film phase on Cu-bearing grains in H2S-rich conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Cu/H2S-mediated reductive elimination removes the hydroxyl group and yields the deoxygenated thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) showed Cu/H2S-mediated reductive dehydroxylation of the hydroxy-thioamide. This is a key carbon-skeleton editing step, but it is also yield-sensitive because it depends on the contested availability of reduced copper at the surface.

reactions.name: Thioamide-to-nitrile exchange to 2-(4-cyano-4-hydroxybutyl)guanidine

conditions.other: HCN recharge during the wet phase of cyanosulfidic pool cycling.

reactions.mechanism: Thioamide hydrolysis-exchange coupled to HCN installation of a new nitrile regenerates a terminal cyanohydrin and releases ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: The complex thioamide-to-nitrile and cyanohydrin exchange was reported by Patel et al. (2015) and exemplifies the nitrile-thioamide redox cycling of cyanosulfidic chemistry. Because the mechanistic sequence is multistage, this is plausibly one of the more selectivity-limited yield bottlenecks in the network.

reactions.name: Amination of the cyanohydrin-guanidine to the alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: NH3-rich concentrated pool after evaporation of ammonium-bearing solutions.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonolysis of the cyanohydrin center converts the hydroxyl-bearing nitrile into the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) placed this amination late in the arginine sequence because it directly installs the alpha-amino group needed for the amino acid while leaving the guanidine side chain intact. The step is chemically attractive because it avoids requiring a separate prebiotic transamination chemistry.

reactions.name: Aqueous hydrolysis of the alpha-aminonitrile to arginine

conditions.other: Repeated heating/cooling and wet-dry cycling promote hydration and hydrolysis; no chiral selection is implied.

reactions.mechanism: Stepwise nitrile hydration and hydrolysis, via an amide-level intermediate, converts the aminonitrile into the amino acid and releases ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) completed the sequence by aqueous nitrile hydrolysis to arginine. The chemistry is standard for aminonitriles, but it should furnish racemic arginine rather than enantioenriched L-arginine, and the literature highlights low cumulative multistep yield as a major accumulation challenge.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Conceptually this tracks Patel et al. well, but the encoded chemistry is not valid enough. rxn_004 is a major conservation failure: the dry cyclization creates an O-containing product and changes N count with no balanced reagent or byproduct set. rxn_009 and rxn_010 are also unbalanced. rxn_011 likely needs H2O as a product, and rxn_012 needs 2 H2O as reactants. The route is coherent but not executable as written.
suggestions: Re-specify rxn_004 with full stoichiometric reagents and byproducts; a dry step cannot yield mol_009 as written without an explicit O source and corrected N accounting.
Rework rxn_009 and rxn_010 with explicit Cu/H2S/H2O redox bookkeeping, or verify the formulas of mol_011 to mol_013.
Add H2O as a product in rxn_011 and 2 H2O as reactants in rxn_012.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is connected, uses molecule IDs consistently, and conceptually aligns strongly with the Patel et al. surface cyanosulfidic arginine chemistry while appropriately avoiding unsupported detours. The hub intermediates and route logic are coherent, and the all-surface environmental framing is generally plausible. However, the deterministic balance check is fatal to approval: only 5 of 12 reactions are balanced as written, and 7 are unbalanced. The most serious issues are rxn_004 to rxn_006 for cyclization to mol_009, where no single small-species fix resolves the conservation problem and the dry variant lacks any explicit O source; rxn_009, which appears to involve a formula or stoichiometry inconsistency rather than a simple missing water; rxn_010, which likely omits key species such as H2O and H2S but still needs full rebalancing; rxn_011, which should include H2O as a product; and rxn_012, which should include 2 H2O as reactants. The narrative also aligns reasonably with the literature in acknowledging racemic output and copper dependence as known challenges. P10 is the least flawed listed fragment, while P2 is the strongest complete feedstock-to-target route, but the network cannot be approved until the seven unbalanced steps are corrected.
